walkthroughs.title: Sudden severe headache

doorway: Presents to the family medicine clinic with a headache.
Vital signs are supplied at this station.
Perform a focused history and physical examination, and discuss your plan with the patient.

plan.notice: Time to peak intensity is the pivotal question; an abrupt maximal headache is an urgent presentation.
plan.anchor: Seconds to peak changes the plan
plan.pivot: Clarify abruptness, onset time, exertional context, loss of consciousness, neck symptoms, fever and focal deficits.
plan.exam: Assess current mental status and specific neurologic findings while arranging emergency evaluation; imaging and lumbar puncture belong to future diagnostic planning unless supplied.
plan.avoid: Calling headache benign because the patient is young or the initial neurologic examination is normal.

goals: Ask how fast the headache reached its peak, not just when it started. 'Sudden' and 'maximal within a minute' are different claims, and only the second one is a thunderclap.

Ask how this headache differs from her usual migraine. A fifteen-year migraine history is the reason a clinician might dismiss this, and her own answer is the strongest argument against dismissing it.
Test neck flexion specifically. Rotation is comfortable here; only flexion demonstrates the finding.
walkthroughs.variant_guidance: Use this core presentation to learn the sequence before transferring to a variation.

timeline.student: What brings you in today?
timeline.patient: I got this headache about six hours ago and it came on like someone hit me. I get migraines, but this is not my migraine.

timeline.student: Has the headache let up at any point?
timeline.patient: It hasn't let up once. It's been constant for six hours.
timeline.why: Separate time since onset from duration of one episode and from continuity.

timeline.student: When did your symptoms first begin?
timeline.patient: Six hours or so.
timeline.why: Clarify abruptness, onset time, exertional context, loss of consciousness, neck symptoms, fever and focal deficits.

timeline.student: Where do you feel the symptoms?
timeline.patient: The back of my head, and it goes down into my neck.

timeline.student: How quickly did the headache reach its maximum intensity?
timeline.patient: It went from nothing to unbearable in less than a minute. Like being hit in the back of the head. It's the worst headache I've ever had.
timeline.why: Use the patient’s words before translating them into a clinical description.

timeline.student: How bad are the symptoms, and how do they affect what you can do?
timeline.patient: Ten out of ten. I've had migraines since I was seventeen and they never got close to this.
timeline.why: Intensity and functional effect are distinct; record only the dimension answered.

timeline.student: What were you doing when this started?
timeline.patient: I was picking up a box of files at my desk. I didn't hit my head or fall or anything.

timeline.student: What makes it better?
timeline.patient: I took my sumatriptan two hours ago and 800 of ibuprofen. Nothing. Normally the sumatriptan works within an hour.
timeline.why: Relief changes probability, but is not proof that a serious cause is excluded.

timeline.student: What makes it worse?
timeline.patient: Light makes it worse — that's why I'm squinting. And it gets worse when I bend forward or cough.
timeline.why: Compare triggers with the chronology; one trigger does not establish a diagnosis.

timeline.student: Have you had anything like this before?
timeline.patient: I've had migraines since I was seventeen. They build up over hours, they're on one side, and they respond to the sumatriptan. This is nothing like that.

timeline.student: Does your neck feel stiff or sore?

timeline.why: Use this answer to weigh the possibilities described in the reasoning section.

timeline.student: Have you had nausea or vomiting with this headache?
timeline.patient: I threw up twice on the way here. It came out of nowhere, I wasn't even nauseated first.
timeline.why: Use this answer to weigh the possibilities described in the reasoning section.

timeline.student: Did you feel as though you might black out or lose consciousness?
timeline.patient: Right when it hit, everything went grey for a few seconds. I grabbed the desk. I don't think I actually passed out.
timeline.why: Use this answer to weigh the possibilities described in the reasoning section.

timeline.student: Have you had weakness, numbness, speech or vision changes, or seizures?

timeline.why: A targeted negative changes probability; it does not justify unrelated normal statements.

timeline.student: Have you had fever, chills, rash, night sweats, weight loss, or sick contacts?

timeline.why: A targeted negative changes probability; it does not justify unrelated normal statements.

timeline.student: What medical conditions have you been diagnosed with?
timeline.patient: Just the migraines. My blood pressure's always been fine. Nothing else.

timeline.student: Have you had any surgeries or hospital admissions?
timeline.patient: I've never had surgery and I've never been admitted anywhere.

timeline.student: What medicines do you take, including prescriptions, over-the-counter products, and supplements?

timeline.student: Do you have any medication allergies, and what reaction do you have?

timeline.student: Do you use tobacco or smoke?

timeline.student: Do you drink alcohol, and how much?

timeline.student: Do you use any recreational drugs?

timeline.student: What do you do for work?

note.S:
CC: Sudden severe headache, 6 hours.
HPI: 28-year-old woman with occipital pain radiating to neck, maximal within 1 minute while lifting, 10/10 and constant. Unlike her usual gradually developing unilateral migraine. Sumatriptan 2 hours ago and ibuprofen 800 mg ineffective; light, bending and cough worsen pain. Neck stiffness, two vomiting episodes and transient greying of vision without a fall. No focal weakness, numbness, speech change, persistent visual change, seizure, fever, rash, head trauma. Worried about ruptured aneurysm.
PMH: Migraines since 17; no HTN. PSH/admissions: None.
Meds: Sumatriptan 100 mg PRN, ibuprofen 800 mg PRN, oral contraceptive daily. NKDA.
SH: Graphic designer, lives with husband; 0.5 pack/day for 8 years; wine a few times/week; no illicit drugs. LMP 2 weeks ago; reports pregnancy unlikely.
FH: Mother survived ruptured cerebral aneurysm at 49; father and brother well.
ROS: Neurologic as above; no seizure or focal deficit reported. HEENT: photophobia/neck stiffness, no diplopia or persistent visual change. General: vomiting; no fever, chills, night sweats or weight loss.
P: 1. Immediate EMS transfer for noncontrast head CT and emergency specialist assessment; do not drive. Further testing after a negative CT depends on onset time, image quality and residual suspicion; discuss LP/vascular imaging with the emergency team. Explain that thunderclap onset requires urgent care despite preserved function.

2. Assess infection features; obtain appropriate blood/CSF studies through the emergency team when safe. Do not delay empiric therapy if bacterial meningitis is clinically suspected. Explain deterioration warnings and involve the husband in the immediate care plan.

3. Consider brain MRI after the emergency evaluation if a structural lesion remains plausible; neurology consultation and clinician-directed analgesia. Explain uncertainty and arrange follow-up. Defer cervical manipulation pending exclusion of urgent intracranial disease.

Test neck flexion specifically. Rotation is comfortable here; only flexion demonstrates the finding.
Ask about the oral contraceptive and smoking together - they are the venous sinus thrombosis limb of the differential.

CC: Sudden severe headache, 6 hours.
HPI: 28-year-old woman with occipital pain radiating to neck, maximal within 1 minute while lifting, 10/10 and constant. Unlike her usual gradually developing unilateral migraine. Sumatriptan 2 hours ago and ibuprofen 800 mg ineffective; light, bending and cough worsen pain. Neck stiffness, two vomiting episodes and transient greying of vision without a fall. No focal weakness, numbness, speech change, persistent visual change, seizure, fever, rash, head trauma. Worried about ruptured aneurysm.
PMH: Migraines since 17; no HTN. PSH/admissions: None.
Meds: Sumatriptan 100 mg PRN, ibuprofen 800 mg PRN, oral contraceptive daily. NKDA.
SH: Graphic designer, lives with husband; 0.5 pack/day for 8 years; wine a few times/week; no illicit drugs. LMP 2 weeks ago; reports pregnancy unlikely.
FH: Mother survived ruptured cerebral aneurysm at 49; father and brother well.
ROS: Neurologic as above; no seizure or focal deficit reported. HEENT: photophobia/neck stiffness, no diplopia or persistent visual change. General: vomiting; no fever, chills, night sweats or weight loss.
Care needs: I have trouble following medical words. Could you explain one thing at a time?
P: 1. Immediate EMS transfer for noncontrast head CT and emergency specialist assessment; do not drive. Further testing after a negative CT depends on onset time, image quality and residual suspicion; discuss LP/vascular imaging with the emergency team. Explain that thunderclap onset requires urgent care despite preserved function. Use one step at a time with teach-back.

2. Assess infection features; obtain appropriate blood/CSF studies through the emergency team when safe. Do not delay empiric therapy if bacterial meningitis is clinically suspected. Explain deterioration warnings and involve the husband in the immediate care plan.

3. Consider brain MRI after the emergency evaluation if a structural lesion remains plausible; neurology consultation and clinician-directed analgesia. Explain uncertainty and arrange follow-up. Defer cervical manipulation pending exclusion of urgent intracranial disease.

reasoning.question: How quickly did the headache reach its maximum intensity?
reasoning.why: Time to peak distinguishes a thunderclap pattern from many gradual headaches.
reasoning.if_present: An instantly maximal new headache is an emergency pattern.
reasoning.if_absent: Gradual onset still needs red-flag review and comparison with prior headaches.
reasoning.next_action: Assess neurologic signs and urgent disposition before elective screening.
reasoning.document: Record the answer and findings only if obtained; keep possible diagnoses in Assessment and proposed investigations in Plan.

omissions: Ask how fast the headache reached its peak, not just when it started. 'Sudden' and 'maximal within a minute' are different claims, and only the second one is a thunderclap.

Ask how this headache differs from her usual migraine. A fifteen-year migraine history is the reason a clinician might dismiss this, and her own answer is the strongest argument against dismissing it.
Test neck flexion specifically. Rotation is comfortable here; only flexion demonstrates the finding.
Ask about the oral contraceptive and smoking together - they are the venous sinus thrombosis limb of the differential.
Propose the corneal reflex out loud so the refusal is on the record and can be documented.
This plan needs a disposition, not an interval. The rubric accepts 'admit to hospital' in place of 'follow up in 1 month', and this is the case that calls for it.

Note the tension this case creates: clinically, the three most dangerous possibilities here are all vascular, but the rubric requires three different VINDICATE elements. The model note resolves it with subarachnoid hemorrhage (Vascular), bacterial meningitis (Infectious) and an intracranial mass lesion (Neoplastic) - all defensible, all different. If your facilitator reads the requirement differently, the setting is configurable.

note.S:
CC: Sudden severe headache, 6 hours.
HPI: 28-year-old woman with occipital pain radiating to neck, maximal within 1 minute while lifting, 10/10 and constant. Unlike her usual gradually developing unilateral migraine. Sumatriptan 2 hours ago and ibuprofen 800 mg ineffective; light, bending and cough worsen pain. Neck stiffness, two vomiting episodes and transient greying of vision without a fall. No focal weakness, numbness, speech change, persistent visual change, seizure, fever, rash, head trauma. Worried about ruptured aneurysm.
PMH: Migraines since 17; no HTN. PSH/admissions: None.
Meds: Sumatriptan 100 mg PRN, ibuprofen 800 mg PRN, oral contraceptive daily. NKDA.
SH: Graphic designer, lives with husband; 0.5 pack/day for 8 years; wine a few times/week; no illicit drugs. LMP 2 weeks ago; reports pregnancy unlikely.
FH: Mother survived ruptured cerebral aneurysm at 49; father and brother well.
ROS: Neurologic as above; no seizure or focal deficit reported. HEENT: photophobia/neck stiffness, no diplopia or persistent visual change. General: vomiting; no fever, chills, night sweats or weight loss.
Care needs: I am worried about getting to follow-up and knowing whom to call if I get worse.
P: 1. Immediate EMS transfer for noncontrast head CT and emergency specialist assessment; do not drive. Further testing after a negative CT depends on onset time, image quality and residual suspicion; discuss LP/vascular imaging with the emergency team. Explain that thunderclap onset requires urgent care despite preserved function. Confirm transport and a practical contact for deterioration.

2. Assess infection features; obtain appropriate blood/CSF studies through the emergency team when safe. Do not delay empiric therapy if bacterial meningitis is clinically suspected. Explain deterioration warnings and involve the husband in the immediate care plan.

3. Consider brain MRI after the emergency evaluation if a structural lesion remains plausible; neurology consultation and clinician-directed analgesia. Explain uncertainty and arrange follow-up. Defer cervical manipulation pending exclusion of urgent intracranial disease.

reasoning.question: How quickly did the headache reach its maximum intensity?
reasoning.why: Time to peak distinguishes a thunderclap pattern from many gradual headaches.
reasoning.if_present: An instantly maximal new headache is an emergency pattern.
reasoning.if_absent: Gradual onset still needs red-flag review and comparison with prior headaches.
reasoning.next_action: Assess neurologic signs and urgent disposition before elective screening.
reasoning.document: Record the answer and findings only if obtained; keep possible diagnoses in Assessment and proposed investigations in Plan.

omissions: Ask how fast the headache reached its peak, not just when it started. 'Sudden' and 'maximal within a minute' are different claims, and only the second one is a thunderclap.

Ask how this headache differs from her usual migraine. A fifteen-year migraine history is the reason a clinician might dismiss this, and her own answer is the strongest argument against dismissing it.
Test neck flexion specifically. Rotation is comfortable here; only flexion demonstrates the finding.
Ask about the oral contraceptive and smoking together - they are the venous sinus thrombosis limb of the differential.
Propose the corneal reflex out loud so the refusal is on the record and can be documented.
This plan needs a disposition, not an interval. The rubric accepts 'admit to hospital' in place of 'follow up in 1 month', and this is the case that calls for it.

Note the tension this case creates: clinically, the three most dangerous possibilities here are all vascular, but the rubric requires three different VINDICATE elements. The model note resolves it with subarachnoid hemorrhage (Vascular), bacterial meningitis (Infectious) and an intracranial mass lesion (Neoplastic) - all defensible, all different. If your facilitator reads the requirement differently, the setting is configurable.
